hints: The median only depends on the middle of the sorted data. Could you split the numbers into a 'smaller half' and a 'bigger half' and just watch where they meet?
Use two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced so their sizes differ by at most one.

1. addNum: push into the lower max-heap.
  2. Move the lower heap's top into the upper min-heap (keeps halves ordered).
  3. If the upper heap is now bigger, move its top back to the lower heap.
  4. findMedian: if the lower heap is bigger, return its top; else return the average of both tops.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Store all numbers; sort on every findMedian call (or keep a sorted list with insertion).
approaches.time: O(n log n) per query (or O(n) per add)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two heaps holding the lower and upper halves; the median is read from their tops.

explain: Add 6: it passes through the upper heap and returns, so lower = {6}, median 6.0. Add 2: lower {2}, upper {6}, median (2+6)/2 = 4.0. Add 9: 9 goes up to upper giving {6,9}; upper is bigger, so 6 moves back, lower {2,6}, median 6.0. Invariant: every number in the lower heap is ≤ every number in the upper heap, and lower has the same size or one more. Edge case: use long or doubles when averaging the two tops.
recognize: A stream of numbers with 'median so far' queries → two balanced heaps (max-heap low half, min-heap high half).
